topic.title: Associative Memory, Sequence Recall, and Forgetting
topic.overview: Associative memory retrieves stored content from partial cues, but capacity and interference determine whether old information survives new learning. This topic includes attractor networks, key-value memories, sequence storage, and biologically inspired scaffolds. Related analyses study how changes to modern neural representations can trigger catastrophic forgetting.
topic.whyItMatters: A memory system should degrade gracefully when its capacity is exceeded rather than abruptly lose everything. Separating stable internal organization from the content attached to it offers one route to balancing storage, recall fidelity, and continued learning.
topic.evolution: The earliest representatives model olfactory and sparse distributed memory. Later work studies correlations, kernel memories, and biological key-value learning. Recent examples introduce fixed scaffolds for graceful recall, long-sequence Hopfield models, temporal-context reinstatement, and theoretical phase changes in forgetting under low-rank adaptation.
openQuestions: How can memory capacity be measured when partial recall remains useful?
Which interventions preserve old associations without blocking the acquisition of new ones?
